entities.description: Card 1 in the Etteilla system. Unlike all other tarot systems, Etteilla placed a unique card at position 1 representing the Questioner — the person consulting the oracle. This card stands for the inquirer themselves: their concerns, their question, their current state. When it appears in a reading it draws attention back to the self and the nature of the inquiry, and in some interpretations also represents the role of the diviner as mediator between seeker and cosmos.

Card 2 in the Etteilla system, corresponding to the Sun. Etteilla positioned this card near the start of his cosmogonic sequence, reflecting divine light as the primal creative force illuminating existence. Where RWS depicts a joyful child on horseback, Etteilla's version emphasises enlightenment, clarity, and the source of all life as a torch that banishes darkness.

Card 3 in the Etteilla system. Etteilla placed the Moon second in his creation sequence after the Sun, emphasising its role as the reflector of divine light and ruler of the tidal, subconscious realm. His divinatory meaning leaned toward deception and hidden enemies more than the RWS version, reflecting a more literally predictive, warning-oriented approach to this card.

Card 4 in the Etteilla system, corresponding to The Star. Etteilla titled this card 'The Stars' (plural), connecting it to the fixed stars and celestial influences in his Egyptian-origin theory of tarot. It retains the hopeful, renewing quality of the RWS Star but with a broader cosmological scope, representing the guiding lights that orient the soul in darkness.

Card 5 in the Etteilla system, corresponding to Judgement. Etteilla called it 'The Trumpets' or 'The Last Judgment', placing it in his cosmogonic sequence as the great awakening call following cosmic creation. It retains the RWS themes of rebirth and reckoning but Etteilla emphasised its literal divinatory meaning of significant news, callings, and decisive moments that cannot be reversed.

Card 6 in the Etteilla system. Etteilla retained the Wheel of Fortune's core meaning of cyclical destiny and fate, situating it as a pivot point in his cosmogonic narrative between the celestial trumpets and the earthly tower. He emphasised the literal turn of fortune in worldly affairs — luck, good timing, and the unpredictable rotation of circumstances.

Card 7 in the Etteilla system, corresponding to The Tower. Etteilla's version of this card preserved the dramatic imagery of sudden destruction and placed it earlier in the sequence than RWS, reflecting its role in his narrative as the disruption of earthly structures after cosmic forces have been set in motion. He read it as misery, poverty, and catastrophic ruin — less metaphorical than RWS.

Card 8 in the Etteilla system. Etteilla kept Temperance at a similar position to later traditions, reading it as the virtue of moderation applied to practical life: prudence in spending, restraint in passions, and careful management of affairs. He diverged from later occult interpretations by keeping the meaning firmly anchored in moral virtue and measured conduct rather than alchemical symbolism.

Card 9 in the Etteilla system. Etteilla's Strength card carried more literal meaning than the RWS version — representing physical power, boldness, and courageous action in the world rather than the gentle inner mastery depicted by Waite. In his divinatory practice it often signified a strong person in the querent's life, or the need for decisive, forceful intervention.

Card 10 in the Etteilla system. Etteilla's Hermit represented the traitor, hypocrite, or dissembler more than the wise solitary seeker of the RWS tradition — a distinctly more suspicious, divinatory reading of solitude and concealment. This reflects Etteilla's emphasis on practical warning: the isolated figure is not merely contemplative but potentially hiding something, a deceiver or false friend.

Card 11 in the Etteilla system. Etteilla read the Hanged Man as prudence and sacrifice — a deliberate suspension of action for a wise purpose rather than the passive surrender emphasised in RWS. In its reversed form it signified a crowd or gathering of people. The card's placement here gives it a pivotal role as the midpoint of the major sequence, the wise pause before transformation.

Card 12 in the Etteilla system. Etteilla's Justice card carried the same core meaning as in other systems — equity, legal proceedings, and impartial judgement — but was placed earlier in his sequence than in RWS. He particularly emphasised it in the context of legal disputes, contracts, and official processes, making it one of the most literally practical cards in his divinatory vocabulary.

Card 13 in the Etteilla system, corresponding to La Papesse. Etteilla retained the female papal figure of the Marseille tradition and interpreted her as embodying gnosis, hidden wisdom, and occult knowledge — appropriate given his Egyptian origin theory. Unlike RWS which submerged her in lunar mystery, Etteilla's Papesse was more explicitly associated with the initiated teacher and keeper of secret doctrines.

Card 14 in the Etteilla system, corresponding to Le Pape. Etteilla retained the Pope figure and interpreted it through his esoteric lens as the external religious authority in contrast to the inner gnosis of La Papesse. In practice he read it as orthodox religion, marriage ceremonies, official blessing, and the sanction of established institutions — a card of formal, public spiritual authority.

Card 15 in the Etteilla system, corresponding to Le Bateleur. Etteilla placed the Magician late in his sequence — not at the beginning as in RWS — reflecting his reordering of the cosmogonic narrative where the craftsman and conjurer appears after cosmic forces have been established. Etteilla read him as sickness or illness in the upright position, a strikingly different meaning from the skilled will-worker of the RWS system.

Card 16 in the Etteilla system. Etteilla's Death card shared the transformative meaning of later traditions but was more directly predictive of physical mortality in some readings, reflecting his practical divinatory orientation. In his system Death could literally indicate serious illness or the death of someone close, though its broader meaning of endings and transformation was also present.

Card 17 in the Etteilla system. Etteilla's Devil represented force majeure, overwhelming external power, and the black arts — a more externally threatening figure than the RWS Devil's focus on internal bondage and addiction. He read this card as violence, force, and fatality in worldly affairs, giving it a menacing, literal interpretation aligned with his practical predictive system.

Card 18 in the Etteilla system. Etteilla read the Lovers as representing romantic attachment and the choice between love and duty more concretely than RWS. He associated it specifically with engagement, courtship, and the pull of desire in human affairs. In a reading it frequently pointed to an actual romantic situation in the querent's life rather than a broad philosophical choice.

Card 19 in the Etteilla system. Etteilla's Chariot was read as help arriving from outside, relief from adversity, and assistance that comes unexpectedly to carry the querent forward — a meaning subtly different from the RWS interpretation of wilful self-mastery and triumph through personal control. It often indicated a vehicle, a journey, or a person coming to one's aid.

Card 20 in the Etteilla system. Etteilla's Emperor occupied a later position in the sequence than in RWS, but retained the meaning of authority, stability, and masculine power in practical affairs. He represented a powerful father-figure, patron, or sovereign — a concrete person of high status rather than an abstract archetype, consistent with Etteilla's more personal, situational reading style.

Card 21 in the Etteilla system. Etteilla placed the Empress near the end of his major arcana sequence, representing the feminine counterpart to the Emperor: a powerful woman, mother figure, or influential female patron. His interpretation was resolutely practical, identifying her with action, motion, and decisive feminine authority in real-world affairs.

Card 22 in the Etteilla system. The World closes Etteilla's major arcana sequence as completion, fullness, and the integration of all that has come before — the cosmic narrative returning to wholeness. Etteilla interpreted it as travel, journey, and worldly success, keeping its positive, culminating meaning while grounding it in practical outcomes rather than mystical integration.
